label: Concentration of Measure
notes: This chapter, printed pages 567 through 628, turns transport inequalities into visible tail bounds. The central theme is that a single curvature lower bound forces every Lipschitz function to cluster sharply around its mean, and the optimal-transport route through Talagrand's inequality makes that mechanism transparent and quantitative for the learner.

label: The Concentration Phenomenon
notes: In high dimension a one-Lipschitz function barely moves: its values pile up within a few standard deviations of the median while the surviving probability decays like a Gaussian tail. We motivate why dimension, not luck, produces this rigidity, and why positive curvature is the structural cause behind the entire phenomenon.

label: Talagrand's T2 Inequality
notes: Talagrand's transport-entropy inequality bounds the squared quadratic Wasserstein distance from any probability measure to the reference by twice its relative entropy divided by the curvature constant. We read each symbol carefully and stress that the same constant K controls both the transport cost and the eventual strength of the concentration we derive.

label: Entropy Controls Transport
notes: The right side measures how far a competitor density sits from equilibrium in information; the left side measures the geometric cost of physically transporting equilibrium onto it. T2 asserts that cheap entropy forbids expensive transport, so distributions close in entropy simply cannot drift far away in Wasserstein distance.

label: CD(K,infinity) Gives T2
notes: Under the curvature-dimension condition with positive K and infinite dimension, the reference measure satisfies T2 with that same K. We sketch how a Ricci lower bound, encoded through displacement convexity of entropy along Wasserstein geodesics, propagates into the transport-entropy estimate without any additional smoothness or structural hypotheses.

label: The Logarithmic Sobolev Inequality
notes: The log-Sobolev inequality bounds the entropy of a density by its Fisher information up to the constant one over two K. It sits one rung above Talagrand: differentiating along the heat flow turns Fisher information into the engine that drives entropy decay and ultimately yields the transport bound we want.

label: From LSI down to T2
notes: Otto and Villani showed the logarithmic Sobolev inequality implies Talagrand's T2 with the identical constant, by integrating the Hamilton-Jacobi semigroup along a Wasserstein geodesic. The converse generally fails, so T2 is strictly weaker, sitting between the Poincaré inequality and the full log-Sobolev inequality in the hierarchy.

label: Marton's Argument
notes: Marton's coupling argument converts any T2 measure directly into concentration. Bounding the transport distance between the conditioned measure on a set and the conditioned measure on its enlargement's complement, then applying Pinsker-type entropy control, yields an exponential bound on the complement of a neighbourhood without ever differentiating a function.

label: Bobkov-Gotze Duality
notes: Bobkov and Götze recast T2 through Kantorovich duality: the transport inequality is equivalent to a sub-Gaussian bound on the Laplace transform of every one-Lipschitz function. This dual reading is exactly what makes the median tail estimate fall out mechanically from a single curvature constant, with no further geometric input required.

label: Gaussian-Thin Tails
notes: Combining the dual bound with Chebyshev's exponential trick gives the headline estimate: a one-Lipschitz function exceeds its mean by r with probability at most the exponential of minus K r squared over two. The tails are genuinely Gaussian in shape, with width governed by curvature rather than by dimension.

label: Reading the Diagnostic
notes: The notebook plots the empirical Lipschitz tail against the Talagrand bound on one axis and checks that the bound curve stays above the data everywhere. We connect that numerical invariant back to the theory: a passing check is precisely the computational footprint of the curvature constant doing its concentration work in practice.

label: Synthesis and Outlook
notes: We close by assembling the chain: curvature gives the log-Sobolev inequality, which gives Talagrand T2, which through Marton and Bobkov-Götze gives Gaussian concentration of Lipschitz functions. The dimension-free constant K is the single thread, and the same machinery extends to the CD(K,N) finite-dimensional setting with sharpened constants.
